text: Bet a dollar on red a thousand times. Only one in twenty-two people end up ahead.
An American roulette wheel has thirty-eight slots.
Eighteen are red, and eighteen are black.
And two are green: zero and double zero.
Bet red: win, you get a dollar. Lose, it's gone.
Sounds like a coin flip, right? Almost— but not quite.
Hit like if you thought it was fifty-fifty.
Red only hits eighteen times out of thirty-eight, about forty-seven percent.
That gap is the house edge, the casino's built-in cut.
On average, it eats just over five cents per dollar.
Now watch what happens the longer you play.
Send this to the friend who always says, just one more spin.
After ten spins, about thirty-one percent of players are ahead.
After a hundred spins, it's about twenty-six percent.
After five hundred, only eleven percent.
And after a thousand spins? About four and a half percent.
Follow if you'd rather know the odds before the wheel does.
So about one in twenty-two ends up ahead, one kid in a class.
The average player? Down about fifty-three bucks.
Every spin feels almost fair. A thousand of them aren't.
How many spins of red before you walk away?
